_note: The F22 differential corpus, read IN PLACE by crates/embedded-tree's tests and by app/tests/platform/embedded-tree.test.ts. It publishes file CONTENT rather than digests on purpose: a corpus of digests would never exercise either side's hash function, and the two implementations agreeing on a comparison they both skipped is not agreement. Each side hashes `tree` itself and must reproduce `perFileHashes`.

cases.name: clean — every pinned file present and identical
cases.why: The negative control. Without it the corpus proves only that everything is rejected.

cases.name: changed — one file's bytes differ from its pin
cases.why: The tamper everybody thinks of. The other two are the ones that ship.

cases.name: missing — a pinned file is not in the build
cases.why: A build that dropped a file still runs, and fails at the user on the path that needed it.

cases.name: unexpected — a file nobody signed is in the build
cases.why: The direction a manifest-driven loop cannot see: everything the manifest lists is in order, and a payload sits beside it.

cases.name: all three at once, counted separately
cases.why: A report that collapsed to one finding would still pass each single-direction case above.

cases.name: rooted asset keys meet release-relative pins
cases.why: Tauri's AssetKey is rooted (`/index.html`) and release.json is not. If only one side normalised, every file here would be reported as BOTH missing and unexpected — fail-closed, and useless.

cases.name: a same-length near miss is not a match
cases.why: Two files of identical length and one differing byte. A length or size comparison passes this; a digest comparison does not.
